value.overview: The Black-headed Tody-Flycatcher (Todirostrum nigriceps) is a small Neotropical tyrant flycatcher associated mainly with humid lowland forest. It has a striking dark head, pale throat, yellowish underparts, and contrasting wing markings. The species searches actively for small arthropods in leafy vegetation, often in the canopy or along forest edges. Its range extends from Costa Rica and Panama south through parts of Colombia, Venezuela, and western Ecuador.
value.classification: The Black-headed Tody-Flycatcher belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. Its scientific name is Todirostrum nigriceps.
value.identification: This small, active flycatcher has a glossy black or very dark head, a white throat, olive-gray upperparts, and pale yellow to yellowish underparts. The wings show yellowish or olive-edged markings, while the bill is short and relatively broad. It often flicks through foliage with quick movements and may be detected first by its high, thin single-note calls. Care is needed to separate it from other small Todirostrum flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and Panama through northern and eastern Colombia, northwestern Venezuela, and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is primarily a resident of the Caribbean lowlands, locally reaching about 700 meters and occasionally occurring higher, to roughly 1,500 meters. It is uncommon or local on the Pacific side, where it mainly reaches the drainage through low passes in the Cordillera de Guanacaste. It uses very humid lowland forest, forest edges, tall second growth, shaded cacao, and partly open areas with mature trees.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Its local movements may reflect food availability or elevation.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, but in Costa Rica nesting has been reported mainly from March to May. The nest is a short, pear-shaped, pendulous pouch made from pale plant fibers and plant down, with a side entrance protected by a small overhanging visor. It is usually attached 6–15 meters above the ground on a tree at a forest edge or in a partly open site. Nests may be placed near wasp nests, and both adults are believed to participate in construction and parental care.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-headed Tody-Flycatcher feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods. It forages actively among leaves and fine branches, especially in the upper and middle levels of humid forest and at edges. Rather than making long aerial sallies, it typically gleans or makes short advances within vegetation, pausing frequently as it searches. Its small size and quick movements allow it to exploit insects in narrow foliage and shaded forest structure.
value.behavior: It is usually seen alone or in pairs and is an alert, fast-moving bird. Individuals frequently hop or flit through dense foliage, using short calls to maintain contact or advertise. The species can be difficult to observe because it remains among leaves and often moves suddenly from branch to branch. In Costa Rica it may be encountered in forest edges, gardens adjoining mature woodland, shaded farms, and other habitats retaining tall trees.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend has not been quantified reliably.
